<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:local-zero}
Let $p\geq5$ be prime. For every $z\in\mathbb Z$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:a-local-zero}
\delta_p(6z+1)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\delta_p(z)=a(p),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:b-local-zero}
\delta_p(6z+5)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\delta_p(z)=b(p).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:a-identity},
\[
(6z+1)-(6a(p)+1)=6\bigl(z-a(p)\bigr).
\]
Since $p\nmid6$ and $p\mid6a(p)+1$, one has
$p\mid6z+1$ if and only if $p\mid z-a(p)$, which proves
\eqref{eq:a-local-zero}.  The second equivalence follows from
\eqref{eq:b-identity} in the same way.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:six-wheel}
Suppose that $\delta_3(n)=0$. Then
\[
z\longmapsto\{H_z(n),K_z(n)\}
\]
is a bijection from $\mathcal Z(n)$ onto the unordered
representations of $2n$ whose two summands are coprime to $6$.

Suppose that $\delta_3(n)\in\{1,2\}$. Then the same map is
surjective onto the unordered representations of $2n$ whose
summands are coprime to $6$, and its fibers are precisely the
orbits of the involution
\[
\tau_n(z)=m(n)-z.
\]
A fixed parameter exists exactly when $m(n)$ is even. When it
exists, it gives
\[
H_z(n)=K_z(n)=n.
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Every integer coprime to $6$ has canonical remainder $1$ or $5$
under $\delta_6$. Since
\[
\delta_6(2n)
=
\begin{cases}
0, & \delta_3(n)=0,\\
2, & \delta_3(n)=1,\\
4, & \delta_3(n)=2,
\end{cases}
\]
the only possible pairs of canonical residues of two summands
coprime to $6$ are
\[
(1,5)\ \text{or}\ (5,1),
\qquad
(1,1),
\qquad
(5,5),
\]
respectively.

If $\delta_3(n)=0$, exactly one summand has canonical remainder
$1$ under $\delta_6$. Writing that summand uniquely as $6z+1$
gives the first row of \eqref{eq:parametrization-table}. The
positivity conditions give precisely $z\in\mathcal Z(n)$. Hence every
unordered representation occurs exactly once.

If $\delta_3(n)=1$, both summands have canonical remainder $1$.
If $\delta_3(n)=2$, both have canonical remainder $5$. In either
case,
\[
H_{m(n)-z}(n)=K_z(n),
\qquad
K_{m(n)-z}(n)=H_z(n).
\]
Thus interchanging the summands corresponds exactly to replacing
$z$ by $m(n)-z$, and the fibers are the orbits of $\tau_n$.

A fixed parameter satisfies
\[
z=m(n)-z,
\]
or equivalently $2z=m(n)$. At such a parameter,
\eqref{eq:parametrization-sum} gives
\[
H_z(n)=K_z(n)=n.
\]
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:collision}
For every $i\in\{1,\dots,r\}$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:collision}
x_i(n)=y_i(n)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\delta_{p_i}(n)=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Suppose first that $e(n)=0$. By
\eqref{eq:xy-definition}, equality of the two canonical residues
is equivalent to
\[
\delta_{p_i}(a_i)
=
\delta_{p_i}\bigl(m(n)-b_i\bigr).
\]
Using \eqref{eq:delta-divisibility} and
$a_i+b_i=p_i-1$, this is equivalent to
\[
p_i\mid m(n)+1.
\]
Since
\[
n=3\bigl(m(n)+1\bigr)
\]
and $p_i\neq3$, the last condition is equivalent to
$\delta_{p_i}(n)=0$.

Suppose now that $e(n)=1$. Equality of the excluded residues is
equivalent to
\[
p_i\mid m(n)-2a_i.
\]
Since $n=3m(n)+1$,
\[
3\bigl(m(n)-2a_i\bigr)
=
n-\bigl(6a_i+1\bigr).
\]
By \eqref{eq:a-identity}, the quantity $6a_i+1$ is divisible by
$p_i$. Hence
\[
p_i\mid m(n)-2a_i
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p_i\mid n.
\]

Finally, suppose that $e(n)=2$. Equality is now equivalent to
\[
p_i\mid m(n)-2b_i.
\]
Because $n=3m(n)+5$,
\[
3\bigl(m(n)-2b_i\bigr)
=
n-\bigl(6b_i+5\bigr).
\]
The quantity $6b_i+5$ is divisible by $p_i$ by
\eqref{eq:b-identity}. Therefore,
\[
p_i\mid m(n)-2b_i
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p_i\mid n.
\]
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:L-count}
Let $m\geq-1$, let $q\geq1$, and let
$0\leq a\leq q-1$. Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:L-definition}
L(m,q,a)
:=
\#\left\{
z\in\mathbb Z
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
0\leq z\leq m,\ 
\delta_q(z)=a
\right\}
=
1+\left\lfloor\frac{m-a}{q}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
If $a\leq m$, the integers being counted are
\[
a,\ a+q,\ a+2q,\dots
\]
up to $m$, which gives the stated formula.

If $a>m$, then
\[
-1\leq\frac{m-a}{q}<0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
1+\left\lfloor\frac{m-a}{q}\right\rfloor=0.
\]
This includes $m=-1$, for which the interval
$\{z\in\mathbb Z:0\leq z\leq m\}$ is empty.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:exact-formula}
For every positive integer $n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:C-exact}
\mathcal C_P(n)
=
\sum_{\boldsymbol\alpha\in\{0,1,2\}^{r}}
W_{\boldsymbol\alpha}(n)
L\left(
m(n),
Q_{\boldsymbol\alpha},
\eta_{\boldsymbol\alpha}(n)
\right).
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:g-exact}
g_P(2n)
=
\begin{cases}
\mathcal C_P(n),
&
\delta_3(n)=0,
\\[5pt]
\dfrac{\mathcal C_P(n)+F_P(n)}{2},
&
\delta_3(n)\in\{1,2\}.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
For $z\in\mathcal Z(n)$, define
\[
I_i(z)
=
\mathbf 1_{\{
\delta_{p_i}(z)\notin\{x_i(n),y_i(n)\}
\}}.
\]
By \eqref{eq:local-exclusion},
\[
\prod_{i=1}^{r}I_i(z)=1
\]
exactly when
\[
\gcd\bigl(H_z(n)K_z(n),P\bigr)=1.
\]
Therefore,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:C-indicator-sum}
\mathcal C_P(n)
=
\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z(n)}
\prod_{i=1}^{r}I_i(z).
\end{equation}

Expanding each factor by means of
\eqref{eq:local-indicator} gives
\[
\prod_{i=1}^{r}I_i(z)
=
\sum_{\boldsymbol\alpha\in\{0,1,2\}^{r}}
W_{\boldsymbol\alpha}(n)
\mathbf 1_{\{
\delta_{Q_{\boldsymbol\alpha}}(z)
=
\eta_{\boldsymbol\alpha}(n)
\}}.
\]
For $\boldsymbol\alpha=\boldsymbol0$, this indicator is
identically $1$ because
\[
Q_{\boldsymbol0}=1,
\qquad
\eta_{\boldsymbol0}(n)=0,
\qquad
\delta_1(z)=0.
\]

Summing the expansion over $z\in\mathcal Z(n)$ and applying
Lemma~\ref{lem:L-count} gives \eqref{eq:C-exact}.

Suppose that $\delta_3(n)=0$. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:six-wheel}, every admissible parameter
corresponds to exactly one unordered representation. Hence
\[
g_P(2n)=\mathcal C_P(n).
\]

Suppose now that $\delta_3(n)\in\{1,2\}$. The involution
\[
z\longmapsto m(n)-z
\]
preserves admissibility because it interchanges $H_z(n)$ and
$K_z(n)$. Burnside's lemma gives
\[
g_P(2n)
=
\frac{\mathcal C_P(n)+F_P(n)}{2},
\]
provided that $F_P(n)$ is exactly the number of admissible fixed
parameters. We now verify this identification.

A fixed parameter exists exactly when $m(n)$ is even. In the two
cases under consideration,
\[
n=3m(n)+1
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
n=3m(n)+5.
\]
Since both constant terms are odd, $m(n)$ is even exactly when
$n$ is odd. If $\gcd(n,6P)=1$, then $n$ is odd, so the fixed
parameter
\[
z=\frac{m(n)}2
\]
exists and gives $H_z(n)=K_z(n)=n$. It is admissible. Conversely,
every admissible fixed parameter gives the decomposition
$2n=n+n$ and therefore requires $\gcd(n,6P)=1$. Hence the number of admissible fixed parameters is exactly
$F_P(n)$, which proves \eqref{eq:g-exact}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:r-one}
If $r=1$ and $P=p$, then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:r-one-C}
\mathcal C_p(n)
=
m(n)+1
-
\bigl(1-\varepsilon_1(n)\bigr)
L\bigl(m(n),p,x_1(n)\bigr)
-
L\bigl(m(n),p,y_1(n)\bigr).
\end{equation}
Together with \eqref{eq:g-exact}, this specializes the general
formula to an equivalent form of the one-prime result in
\cite{Salazar2026}.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
When $r=1$, the three possible values of $\alpha_1$ are
$0$, $1$, and $2$, with respective weights
\[
1,
\qquad
-(1-\varepsilon_1(n)),
\qquad
-1.
\]
The term corresponding to $\alpha_1=0$ is
\[
L(m(n),1,0)=m(n)+1.
\]
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
For fixed $P$, the inverses in \eqref{eq:eta-explicit} may be
precomputed.  Since $w_{i,1}(n)=0$ exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(n)=1$, the number of terms with nonzero weight in
\eqref{eq:C-exact} is
\[
\prod_{i=1}^{r}\bigl(3-\varepsilon_i(n)\bigr),
\]
and is therefore at most $3^r$. Some of these summands can still
vanish because their interval counts are zero. The expansion is a finite
Legendre-type inclusion--exclusion formula in which the surviving
residue classes are represented explicitly by the Chinese
remainder theorem; compare the classical Legendre sieve
\cite{FriedlanderIwaniec2010}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:R-cardinality}
For every positive integer $n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:R-cardinality}
\theta(2n,M)
=
\#\mathcal R_P(n)
=
\kappa_P(n).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $q$ be a prime divisor of $M$.  The two local coprimality
conditions exclude the residues
\[
0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\delta_q(2n)
\]
under $\delta_q$. They coincide exactly when $q\mid2n$.  Hence the
number of allowed residues is $q-1$ in the collision case and
$q-2$ otherwise.  The factor at $q=2$ is $1$, the factor at
$q=3$ is $1+\mathbf 1_{\{\delta_3(n)=0\}}$, and the factor at
$q=p_i$ is $p_i-2+\varepsilon_i(n)$.  Since $M$ is squarefree,
the Chinese remainder theorem gives the product
\eqref{eq:kappa-definition}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:singular-factor}
One has
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:kappa-singular}
\frac{\kappa_P(n)}{M}
=
\left(\frac{\varphi(M)}{M}\right)^2
\mathfrak S_M^{\mathrm{fin}}(2n).
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:R-cardinality},
\[
\frac{\kappa_P(n)}{M}
=
\prod_{q\mid M}
\left(1-\frac{\nu_q(2n)}q\right),
\]
whereas
\[
\frac{\varphi(M)}M
=
\prod_{q\mid M}\left(1-\frac1q\right).
\]
Factoring the square of the latter local term proves the identity.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:reflection-identity}
For every positive integer $n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:reflection-identity}
2g_P(2n)-F_P(n)
=
\#
\left(
\widetilde{\mathcal R}_P(n)\cap[1,2n]
\right).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:reflection-block-bound}
g_P(2n)
\geq
\frac12
\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{M}\right\rfloor
\kappa_P(n).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Neither $0$ nor $2n$ belongs to
$\widetilde{\mathcal R}_P(n)$.  The involution
$a\mapsto2n-a$ pairs the remaining elements in
$[1,2n]$, except for the fixed point $a=n$, which is present
exactly when $F_P(n)=1$.  The resulting orbits are precisely the
unordered admissible decompositions counted by $g_P(2n)$, proving
\eqref{eq:reflection-identity}.

The interval $[1,2n]$ contains
$\lfloor2n/M\rfloor$ disjoint complete blocks of length $M$.
Each contains $\kappa_P(n)$ elements of the lift.  Applying
\eqref{eq:reflection-identity} and discarding the nonnegative
term $F_P(n)$ gives \eqref{eq:reflection-block-bound}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:half-period-identity}
For every positive integer $n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:half-period-identity}
\begin{aligned}
2g_P\bigl(2(n+3P)\bigr)-F_P(n+3P)
&=2g_P(2n)-F_P(n)+\kappa_P(n).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The shift $n\mapsto n+3P$ changes $2n$ by $M=6P$.
Thus the periodic lifts are identical, while the interval in
\eqref{eq:reflection-identity} gains exactly one complete block of
$M$ integers. This block contains $\kappa_P(n)$ admissible integers.
Subtracting the two reflection identities proves the formula.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:affine-periodicity}
For every positive integer $n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:affine-periodicity}
g_P\bigl(2(n+M)\bigr)-g_P(2n)
=
\kappa_P(n).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The sets
$\widetilde{\mathcal R}_P(n+M)$ and $\widetilde{\mathcal R}_P(n)$ are
identical, because $\delta_M(2M)=0$.  Enlarging
$[1,2n]$ to $[1,2n+2M]$ adds two complete periods and therefore
$2\kappa_P(n)$ elements.  Moreover
$F_P(n+M)=F_P(n)$.  Subtracting the two instances of
\eqref{eq:reflection-identity} gives the result.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:quasipolynomial}
Write uniquely
\[
n=a+tM,
\qquad
1\leq a\leq M,
\qquad
t\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:quasipolynomial}
g_P(2n)
=
g_P(2a)+t\kappa_P(a).
\end{equation}
Hence $M=6P$ is a quasiperiod of the degree-one
quasipolynomial $g_P(2n)$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Iterate Theorem~\ref{thm:affine-periodicity} and use
$\kappa_P(a+jM)=\kappa_P(a)$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:ray-formula}
For every positive integer $t$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ray-formula}
g_P(2tP)
=
\frac{
\left(1+\mathbf 1_{\{\delta_3(t)=0\}}\right)t\varphi(P)
}{6}
+
\frac{\chi_3(t)}{3}
\prod_{i=1}^{r}
\bigl(\chi_3(p_i)-1\bigr).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Put $n=tP$. Formula \eqref{eq:g-short-interval} gives
\[
g_P(2tP)
=
\#\left\{
1\leq h\leq tP
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
\gcd(h,M)=\gcd(2tP-h,M)=1
\right\}.
\]

For every prime $p_i\mid P$,
\[
p_i\mid2tP.
\]
Therefore,
\[
p_i\mid2tP-h
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p_i\mid h.
\]
The same equivalence holds for the prime $2$. Only the
restriction contributed by the prime $3$ depends on
$\delta_3(t)$.

Suppose first that $\delta_3(t)=0$. Write $t=3u$. Then
\[
2tP=uM,
\]
so
\[
\gcd(2tP-h,M)=\gcd(h,M).
\]
Consequently, $g_P(2tP)$ is the number of integers coprime to
$M$ in the interval
\[
1\leq h\leq tP=\frac{uM}{2}.
\]

The reduced residues under $\delta_M$ occur in pairs
\[
c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
M-c.
\]
There is no fixed point: $M/2=3P$ is not coprime to $M$.
Exactly one member of each pair lies in
$[1,M/2]$. Hence
\[
\#\left\{
1\leq h\leq \frac M2
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
\gcd(h,M)=1
\right\}
=
\frac{\varphi(M)}2
=
\varphi(P).
\]
Here $\varphi(M)=2\varphi(P)$ because $M=6P$ and
$\gcd(P,6)=1$.
Dividing the interval $[1,uM/2]$ into complete periods and,
when necessary, one half-period gives
\[
g_P(2tP)
=
\frac{u\varphi(M)}2
=
u\varphi(P)
=
\frac{t\varphi(P)}3.
\]
This is the first term of \eqref{eq:ray-formula}, while the
character term vanishes because $\chi_3(t)=0$.

Suppose now that $\delta_3(t)\neq0$. Since $P$ is coprime to
$3$, one also has $\delta_3(tP)\neq0$. The restrictions at the
primes $2$ and $3$ are equivalent to
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ray-local-conditions}
\delta_2(h)=1,
\qquad
\delta_3(h)=\delta_3(tP).
\end{equation}
Indeed, the first condition says that $h$ is odd. Under
$\delta_3$, the two excluded residues are $0$ and
$\delta_3(2tP)$. If $\delta_3(tP)=1$, the remaining residue is
$1$, and if $\delta_3(tP)=2$, the remaining residue is $2$.

Let $\mu$ denote the M\"obius function. Applying M\"obius inversion
to the condition $\gcd(h,P)=1$ gives
\[
g_P(2tP)
=
\sum_{d\mid P}\mu(d)
\#
\left\{
1\leq h\leq tP
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
d\mid h,\
\delta_2(h)=1,\
\delta_3(h)=\delta_3(tP)
\right\}.
\]

Write
\[
h=d\ell,
\qquad
X_d=\frac{tP}{d}.
\]
Every divisor $d$ of $P$ is coprime to $6$. In particular, $d$
is odd, so the condition under $\delta_2$ becomes
$\delta_2(\ell)=1$. Moreover, $tP=dX_d$, and multiplication by
$d$ is invertible under $\delta_3$. The second condition in
\eqref{eq:ray-local-conditions} therefore becomes
\[
\delta_3(\ell)=\delta_3(X_d).
\]

For every positive integer $X$ satisfying $\delta_3(X)\neq0$,
define
\[
R_6(X)
=
\#
\left\{
1\leq\ell\leq X
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
\delta_2(\ell)=1,\
\delta_3(\ell)=\delta_3(X)
\right\}.
\]
The four possible canonical residues of $X$ under $\delta_6$
give
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\delta_6(X)
& \text{admissible residue of $\ell$ under $\delta_6$}
& R_6(X)\\
\hline
1 & 1 & \dfrac{X+5}{6}\\[4pt]
2 & 5 & \dfrac{X-2}{6}\\[4pt]
4 & 1 & \dfrac{X+2}{6}\\[4pt]
5 & 5 & \dfrac{X+1}{6}
\end{array}
\]
and hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ray-class-count}
R_6(X)
=
\frac X6
+\frac12\mathbf 1_{\{\delta_2(X)=1\}}
+\frac{\chi_3(X)}3.
\end{equation}

Since $P/d$ is odd for every $d\mid P$, one has
\[
\delta_2(X_d)=\delta_2(t).
\]
Substitution of \eqref{eq:ray-class-count} therefore gives
\[
g_P(2tP)
=
\sum_{d\mid P}\mu(d)
\left(
\frac{tP}{6d}
+\frac12\mathbf 1_{\{\delta_2(t)=1\}}
+\frac{\chi_3(tP/d)}3
\right).
\]

Since $P>1$,
\[
\sum_{d\mid P}\mu(d)=0.
\]
Also,
\[
\sum_{d\mid P}\mu(d)\frac{P}{d}
=
\varphi(P),
\]
and the multiplicativity of $\chi_3$ gives
\[
\sum_{d\mid P}
\mu(d)\chi_3(tP/d)
=
\chi_3(t)
\prod_{i=1}^{r}
\bigl(\chi_3(p_i)-1\bigr).
\]
Combining these three identities proves
\eqref{eq:ray-formula}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
For each $i$, the factor $\chi_3(p_i)-1$ is $-2$ when
$\delta_3(p_i)=2$ and $0$ when $\delta_3(p_i)=1$.  Hence the
second term in \eqref{eq:ray-formula} either vanishes or has
absolute value $2^r/3$. If some $p_i$ satisfies $\delta_3(p_i)=1$,
the character correction vanishes for every $t$. If all satisfy
$\delta_3(p_i)=2$, the correction is $(-2)^r\chi_3(t)/3$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:C-density}
For every positive integer $n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:C-density}
\mathcal C_P(n)
=
\frac{m(n)+1}{P}A_P(n)+\mathcal B_P(n),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:B-bound}
\left|\mathcal B_P(n)\right|
<
\prod_{i=1}^{r}
\bigl(3-\varepsilon_i(n)\bigr)-1
\leq3^r-1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
From the local weights,
\[
\sum_{\boldsymbol\alpha\in\{0,1,2\}^r}
\frac{W_{\boldsymbol\alpha}(n)}{Q_{\boldsymbol\alpha}}
=
\prod_{i=1}^{r}
\left(
1-\frac{1-\varepsilon_i(n)}{p_i}-\frac1{p_i}
\right)
=
\frac{A_P(n)}P.
\]
Separating the mean term from each summand of
\eqref{eq:C-exact} gives \eqref{eq:C-density}.

For a nonzero $\boldsymbol\alpha$, write
\[
m(n)+1=vQ_{\boldsymbol\alpha}+s,
\qquad
0\leq s<Q_{\boldsymbol\alpha}.
\]
If $s=0$, every residue class occurs exactly $v$ times in the
parameter interval, so its discrepancy from the mean is zero.
If $s>0$, each residue class occurs either $v$ or $v+1$ times,
and its discrepancy from the mean has absolute value smaller than
$1$.  Therefore
\[
\left|
L\left(m(n),Q_{\boldsymbol\alpha},
\eta_{\boldsymbol\alpha}(n)\right)
-
\frac{m(n)+1}{Q_{\boldsymbol\alpha}}
\right|
<1.
\]
Finally,
\[
\sum_{\boldsymbol\alpha\neq\boldsymbol0}
|W_{\boldsymbol\alpha}(n)|
=
\prod_{i=1}^{r}\bigl(3-\varepsilon_i(n)\bigr)-1,
\]
and the triangle inequality proves \eqref{eq:B-bound}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:refined-discrepancy}
For every positive integer $n$, put
\[
D_P^{\mathrm{ref}}(n)=
\prod_{i=1}^{r}(3-\varepsilon_i(n))
-\prod_{i=1}^{r}\left(1+\frac{2-\varepsilon_i(n)}{p_i}\right).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:refined-B-bound}
|\mathcal B_P(n)|\leq D_P^{\mathrm{ref}}(n)
<\prod_{i=1}^{r}(3-\varepsilon_i(n))-1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Write $m+1=vq+s$, where $0\leq s<q$. If $s=0$, the discrepancy
of each residue count is zero. Otherwise it is either $-s/q$ or
$1-s/q$. Hence, for all integers $m\geq-1$, $q\geq1$, and
$0\leq a<q$,
\[
\left|L(m,q,a)-\frac{m+1}{q}\right|\leq1-\frac1q.
\]
Consequently, the triangle inequality gives
\[
|\mathcal B_P(n)|\leq
\sum_{\boldsymbol\alpha}|W_{\boldsymbol\alpha}(n)|
\left(1-\frac1{Q_{\boldsymbol\alpha}}\right)
=D_P^{\mathrm{ref}}(n).
\]
The equality follows by factoring the two sums of absolute weights.
The term with $\boldsymbol\alpha=\boldsymbol0$ contributes zero.
Since $r\geq1$, the second product defining $D_P^{\mathrm{ref}}(n)$
is strictly greater than $1$, proving the strict inequality.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:density-formula}
For every positive integer $n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:density-formula}
g_P(2n)
=
\frac{n}{M}\kappa_P(n)+\mathcal E_P(n),
\qquad M=6P,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:E-branches}
\mathcal E_P(n)
=
\begin{cases}
\mathcal B_P(n),
&
\delta_3(n)=0,
\\[5pt]
\dfrac{\mathcal B_P(n)+F_P(n)}{2}
+\dfrac{A_P(n)}{3P},
&
\delta_3(n)=1,
\\[9pt]
\dfrac{\mathcal B_P(n)+F_P(n)}{2}
-\dfrac{A_P(n)}{3P},
&
\delta_3(n)=2.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:E-bound}
|\mathcal E_P(n)|<3^r-1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
If $\delta_3(n)=0$, then
$m(n)+1=n/3$, $\kappa_P(n)=2A_P(n)$, and
$g_P(2n)=\mathcal C_P(n)$, which gives the first branch.

If $\delta_3(n)=1$, then
$m(n)+1=(n+2)/3$ and $\kappa_P(n)=A_P(n)$.  Combining
\eqref{eq:g-exact} and \eqref{eq:C-density} gives the second
branch.  The case $\delta_3(n)=2$ is identical with
$m(n)+1=(n-2)/3$ and gives the third branch.

The bound follows from \eqref{eq:B-bound}.  In the two latter
cases,
\[
|\mathcal E_P(n)|
<
\frac{3^r-1}{2}
+\frac12
+\frac13
<
3^r-1,
\]
because $0<A_P(n)/P<1$ and $r\geq1$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
For $P=35$ and $n=20$ one has
\[
g_P(40)=2,
\qquad
\frac{n\kappa_P(n)}{6P}=\frac{40}{21},
\qquad
\mathcal E_P(n)=\frac{2}{21}.
\]
The two admissible representations are
$40=11+29$ and $40=17+23$. Explicitly, $m(20)=5$ and the excluded
residues under $\delta_5$ are $x_1=y_1=0$, while under $\delta_7$
they are $x_2=5$, $y_2=0$. The CRT expansion reduces to
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal C_{35}(20)
&=6-L(5,5,0)-L(5,7,5)-L(5,7,0)\\
&\quad+L(5,35,5)+L(5,35,0)\\
&=6-2-1-1+1+1=4.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $F_{35}(20)=0$, the unordered count is $4/2=2$.
For $P=385$ and $n=14$,
\[
g_P(28)=0,
\qquad
\frac{n\kappa_P(n)}{6P}=\frac{54}{55},
\qquad
\mathcal E_P(n)=-\frac{54}{55}.
\]
Thus a positive local density can coexist with an empty truncated
interval.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:covering}
For every positive integer $n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:covering-equivalence}
g_P(2n)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathcal C_P(n)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathcal Z(n)
\subseteq
\bigcup_{i=1}^{r}\bigl(X_i(n)\cup Y_i(n)\bigr).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The last equivalence follows directly from
\eqref{eq:local-exclusion}.  If $\delta_3(n)=0$, the first
equivalence follows from $g_P(2n)=\mathcal C_P(n)$.  If
$\delta_3(n)\in\{1,2\}$, then
$g_P(2n)=(\mathcal C_P(n)+F_P(n))/2$.  Whenever $F_P(n)=1$, the
central parameter $z=m(n)/2$ is admissible, so
$\mathcal C_P(n)\geq1$.  Hence $\mathcal C_P(n)=0$ forces $F_P(n)=0$,
which proves the first equivalence.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:parameter-density-positive}
If
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:parameter-density-criterion}
\frac{m(n)+1}{P}A_P(n)
\geq
\prod_{i=1}^{r}\bigl(3-\varepsilon_i(n)\bigr)-1,
\end{equation}
then
\[
g_P(2n)>0.
\]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:C-density}, the strict bound
\eqref{eq:B-bound} and hypothesis
\eqref{eq:parameter-density-criterion} give
$\mathcal C_P(n)>0$.  Proposition~\ref{prop:covering} then gives the
result.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:refined-positive}
If $c_P(n)=\#\{i:\delta_{p_i}(n)=0\}$, then
\[
\prod_i(3-\varepsilon_i(n))-1=2^{c_P(n)}3^{r-c_P(n)}-1.
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:refined-discrepancy} also gives the sufficient condition
\[
\frac{m(n)+1}{P}A_P(n)>D_P^{\mathrm{ref}}(n)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g_P(2n)>0.
\]
The strict inequality is required for this inference, because
\eqref{eq:refined-B-bound} can be an equality. For example, when
$P=5$ and $n=10$, one has $\mathcal B_5(10)=D_5^{\mathrm{ref}}(10)=4/5$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:half-period}
For every $n\geq3P$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:half-period-quantitative}
g_P(2n)\geq\frac12\kappa_P(n)
\geq\frac12\prod_{i=1}^{r}(p_i-2)>0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Since $2n\geq M$, one has $\lfloor2n/M\rfloor\geq1$.
Apply \eqref{eq:reflection-block-bound} and the definition of
$\kappa_P(n)$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:residue-free-threshold}
Put
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:T-star-definition}
T^*(P)
=
3(3^r-1)
\prod_{i=1}^{r}\frac{p_i}{p_i-2}
+2.
\end{equation}
If $n\geq T^*(P)$, then $g_P(2n)>0$.
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:T-star-half-period}
T^*(P)\leq3P.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
For every $n$,
\[
m(n)+1\geq\frac{n-2}{3},
\qquad
A_P(n)\geq\prod_{i=1}^{r}(p_i-2),
\]
while
$\prod_i(3-\varepsilon_i(n))-1\leq3^r-1$.
Thus $n\geq T^*(P)$ implies
\eqref{eq:parameter-density-criterion}.

For the second assertion, let
$A_0=\prod_i(p_i-2)$.  Since $A_0\geq3^r$,
\[
T^*(P)
\leq
3P-\frac{P}{3^{r-1}}+2.
\]
Also $P\geq5^r\geq2\cdot3^{r-1}$, so the right-hand side is at
most $3P$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:product-cutoff}
If
\[
P\leq\sqrt{2n},
\]
then $g_P(2n)>0$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
If $P\geq7$, then
$n\geq P^2/2\geq3P\geq T^*(P)$.
For $P=5$, the hypothesis gives $n\geq13$, while
$T^*(5)=12$.  Corollary~\ref{cor:residue-free-threshold}
applies in both cases.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:largest-prime-threshold}
Define
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:N-uniform-definition}
\mathcal N(p)
=
6\bigl(3^{r_p}-1\bigr)
\prod_{\substack{q\ \mathrm{prime}\\5\leq q\leq p}}
\frac{q}{q-2}
+4.
\end{equation}
If $P'>1$ is any squarefree product of primes in $[5,p]$, then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:largest-prime-uniform-positive}
2n\geq\mathcal N(p)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
g_{P'}(2n)>0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Write $P'=q_1\cdots q_s$.  Since $s\leq r_p$ and every factor
$q/(q-2)$ is larger than $1$,
\[
3(3^s-1)
\prod_{j=1}^{s}\frac{q_j}{q_j-2}
+2
\leq
\frac{\mathcal N(p)}2.
\]
Thus $2n\geq\mathcal N(p)$ implies
$n\geq T^*(P')$, and Corollary~\ref{cor:residue-free-threshold}
applies.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:uniform-threshold-asymptotic}
As $p\to\infty$ through the primes,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:N-uniform-asymptotic}
\mathcal N(p)
\sim
\frac{e^{2\gamma}}{2C_2}\,
3^{\pi(p)-2}(\log p)^2,
\end{equation}
and therefore
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:log-N-uniform-asymptotic}
\log\mathcal N(p)
\sim
(\log3)\frac{p}{\log p}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
For every prime $q\geq5$,
\[
1-\frac2q
=
\left(1-\frac1q\right)^2
\left(1-\frac{1}{(q-1)^2}\right).
\]
Mertens' product theorem \cite{HardyWright2008} and the
definition of $C_2$ give
\[
\prod_{\substack{q\ \mathrm{prime}\\5\leq q\leq p}}
\left(1-\frac2q\right)
\sim
\frac{12C_2e^{-2\gamma}}{(\log p)^2}.
\]
Taking reciprocals in this relation and substituting into
\eqref{eq:N-uniform-definition} proves
\eqref{eq:N-uniform-asymptotic}.  The prime number theorem,
$\pi(p)\sim p/\log p$, then gives
\eqref{eq:log-N-uniform-asymptotic}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:three-positivity-scales}
The half-period threshold, uniformly over squarefree products
supported on the primes in $[5,p]$, is
\[
\mathcal H(p)
=
6P_{\leq p}
=
\prod_{q\leq p}q.
\]
Since $T^*(P_{\leq p})\leq3P_{\leq p}$,
\[
\mathcal N(p)\leq\mathcal H(p)
\qquad(p\geq5).
\]
The prime number theorem gives
\[
\log\mathcal H(p)\sim p,
\qquad
\log\mathcal N(p)
\sim
(\log3)\frac{p}{\log p}.
\]
Thus the explicit density threshold is subexponential in $p$,
whereas the half-period threshold has primorial scale.

The natural condition $p\leq\sqrt{2n}$ corresponds to the
quadratic scale $2n\geq p^2$.  Since
$\mathcal N(p)/p^2\to\infty$, the three scales satisfy
\[
p^2=o(\mathcal N(p)),\qquad \mathcal N(p)=o(\mathcal H(p))
\]
as $p\to\infty$.  This comparison records the ranges delivered
by the elementary finite-density argument and the half-period
argument.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:sieve-comparison}
The parameter problem fits the framework of a sieve of dimension
at most $2$. This yields polynomial sufficient scales in the largest
allowed prime, in contrast to the elementary threshold
$\mathcal N(p)$. We record the reason for this comparison.

Put $X=m(n)+1$. For a squarefree divisor $d$ of $P$, the excluded
parameter classes have cardinality
\[
\rho_n(d)=\prod_{q\mid d}(2-\mathbf1_{\{\delta_q(n)=0\}}).
\]
The corresponding interval count is $X\rho_n(d)/d+R_d$, where
$|R_d|\leq\rho_n(d)\leq2^{\omega(d)}$, uniformly in $n$.
Here $\omega(d)$ is the number of distinct prime factors of $d$.
For a uniform lower bound, one may enlarge each excluded set to
exactly two classes at every prime in $[5,p]$, including primes
absent from the original support. Survivors of this more restrictive
sieve are admissible in the original problem. Its local density
is $2/q$, and its remainder is bounded by $2^{\omega(d)}$.
For each fixed integer $K\geq1$, the divisor bound
\[
\sum_{d\leq D}K^{\omega(d)}\ll_K D(1+\log D)^{K-1}
\]
(for integer $K$, by comparison with the $K$-fold divisor function)
controls the weighted remainder sums required by the sieve.
Thus one can use $D=X/(\log X)^B$ with a sufficiently large fixed
$B$.

The DHR lower-bound sieve \cite{DiamondHalberstam2008} has a positive
lower sieve function when $\log D/\log p>\beta_2$, where
$\beta_2\approx4.266$; see the comparison table in \cite{Franze2010}.
Consequently, for each fixed $c>\beta_2$ and all sufficiently large
$p$ (depending on $c$), it gives positivity whenever $2n\geq p^c$,
uniformly over the allowed squarefree products $P'>1$.
Indeed $X\sim n/3$, so this range permits a sieve level with
$\log D/\log p$ bounded strictly above $\beta_2$ and a negligible
weighted remainder. If $X$ is larger, the same argument can be
applied to an initial subinterval of suitable length.

The elementary bound $\mathcal N(p)$ is therefore not an
asymptotically optimal sieve threshold. Its role here is to give
an unconditional, fully explicit inequality for every permitted
finite modulus without additional asymptotic parameters. For each
fixed $c>\beta_2$, the scales satisfy
\[
p^2=o(p^c),\qquad p^c=o(\mathcal N(p)),\qquad
\mathcal N(p)=o(\mathcal H(p)).
\]
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:threshold-table}
The following finite computations compare $T^*(P_{\leq p})=
\mathcal N(p)/2$ with the actual last zero for several small supports.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{r|r|r|r}
$p$ & $\mathcal N(p)/2$ & last $n$ with $g_{P_{\leq p}}(2n)=0$ & $p^2/2$\\
\hline
5 & 12.0 & 8 & 12.5\\
7 & 58.0 & 8 & 24.5\\
11 & 224.4 & 14 & 60.5\\
13 & 810.9 & 14 & 84.5\\
17 & 2775.1 & 20 & 144.5\\
19 & 9325.8 & 28 & 180.5\\
23 & 30665.4 & 32 & 264.5
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The thresholds in the second column are rounded to one decimal
place. The last zeros were obtained by direct integer coprimality
counts for $1\leq n<\lceil T^*(P_{\leq p})\rceil$; the sufficient
threshold excludes every later zero. Monotonicity in the prime
support implies that the last zero for the complete product is
also the maximum last zero over all its nonempty subproducts.
The estimates need not be close to the actual transition:
for example, over $1\leq n\leq6P$, the maximum of $|\mathcal B_P(n)|$
is $12/7$ for $P=35$ and $324/77$ for $P=385$, compared with the
bounds $3^2-1=8$ and $3^3-1=26$.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:cutoff-monotonicity}
Let $P$ and $Q$ be squarefree products of primes at least $5$.
If $P\mid Q$, then, for every positive integer $n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:monotonicity}
g_Q(2n)\leq g_P(2n).
\end{equation}
Consequently, if every prime factor of $P$ is at most
$\sqrt{2n}$, then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cutoff-extremal}
g_{\Pi(n)}(2n)\leq g_P(2n).
\end{equation}
In particular, $g_{\Pi(n)}(2n)>0$ if and only if
$g_P(2n)>0$ for every squarefree product $P$ of primes in the
interval $[5,\sqrt{2n}]$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Every representation whose summands are coprime to $6Q$ also
has both summands coprime to $6P$. Hence the set counted by
$g_Q(2n)$ is contained in the set counted by $g_P(2n)$, which
proves \eqref{eq:monotonicity}. Under the stated cutoff on the
prime factors, one has $P\mid\Pi(n)$, and
\eqref{eq:cutoff-extremal} follows.

For the final assertion, positivity at the complete cutoff
implies positivity for every such $P$ by
\eqref{eq:cutoff-extremal}. The converse follows by taking
$P=\Pi(n)$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:cutoff-prime}
Let $n\geq13$ and let
\[
2\leq u\leq2n-1.
\]
If
\[
\gcd\bigl(u,6\Pi(n)\bigr)=1,
\]
then $u$ is a prime and
\[
u>\sqrt{2n}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Suppose that $u$ is composite. Then $u$ has a prime divisor $q$
satisfying
\[
q\leq\sqrt u<\sqrt{2n}.
\]
If $q\in\{2,3\}$, then
\[
\gcd\bigl(u,6\Pi(n)\bigr)>1.
\]
If $q\geq5$, then $q$ occurs among the prime factors of
$\Pi(n)$, which gives the same contradiction. Therefore $u$
is prime.

It remains to locate this prime. If $u\leq\sqrt{2n}$, then
$u$ itself occurs among the prime factors of $6\Pi(n)$. This
again contradicts the coprimality hypothesis. Hence
$u>\sqrt{2n}$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:cutoff-equivalence}
For $n\geq13$, define
\[
G_{>\sqrt{2n}}(2n)=
\#\left\{(q_1,q_2):
\begin{array}{l}
q_1,q_2\text{ are primes},\\
\sqrt{2n}<q_1\leq q_2,\quad q_1+q_2=2n
\end{array}\right\}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cutoff-exact-count}
g_{\Pi(n)}(2n)=\mathbf1_{\{2n-1\text{ is prime}\}}
+G_{>\sqrt{2n}}(2n).
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cutoff-equivalence}
g_{\Pi(n)}(2n)>0
\iff
\bigl(2n-1\text{ is prime}\bigr)
\ \text{or}\ G_{>\sqrt{2n}}(2n)>0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
An admissible representation with smaller summand $1$ must be
$1+(2n-1)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:cutoff-prime}, it is admissible
exactly when $2n-1$ is prime: in that case $2n-1>\sqrt{2n}$.
Every other admissible representation has both summands at least
$2$. The same proposition shows that both are primes exceeding
$\sqrt{2n}$. Conversely, any such pair consists of two integers
coprime to $6\Pi(n)$. These two disjoint classes of representations
give \eqref{eq:cutoff-exact-count}, and the positivity equivalence
follows.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:additive-prime-cutoff}
Corollary~\ref{cor:cutoff-equivalence} separates the endpoint
$1+(2n-1)$ from the interior of the interval.  When $2n-1$ is
composite, positivity of $g_{\Pi(n)}(2n)$ is equivalent to the
existence of primes $q_1,q_2>\sqrt{2n}$ with
$q_1+q_2=2n$.  When $2n-1$ is prime, the endpoint
$1+(2n-1)$ contributes an additional admissible representation.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:cutoff-product-size}
Let
\[
\vartheta(x)
=
\sum_{\substack{q\leq x\\q\ \mathrm{prime}}}\log q.
\]
Then
\[
\log\Pi(n)
=
\vartheta\bigl(\sqrt{2n}\bigr)-\log6,
\]
so the prime number theorem gives
\[
\Pi(n)
=
\exp\left((1+o(1))\sqrt{2n}\right).
\]
The product cutoff $P\leq\sqrt{2n}$ does not apply to
$P=\Pi(n)$ once the prime $7$ enters the product, that is, from
$n=25$ onward.  Indeed, let $q^+$ denote the next prime after a prime $q$. If
$q\leq\sqrt{2n}<q^+$ with $q\geq7$, Bertrand's postulate \cite{HardyWright2008}
gives $\sqrt{2n}<q^+<2q$, whereas
$\Pi(n)\geq5q>\sqrt{2n}$.

The distinction between a bound on the product $P$ and a bound
on its largest prime is thus substantial.  The uniform threshold
$\mathcal N(p)$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:largest-prime-threshold}
provides an explicit intermediate scale, as summarized in
Remark~\ref{rem:three-positivity-scales}.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:scope-complete-cutoff}
The residue-free threshold and the residue-sensitive criterion
have different scopes. For example, $\mathcal N(5)=24$ guarantees
positivity at the complete cutoff for $13\leq n\leq24$, while
$\mathcal N(7)=116$ gives $58\leq n\leq60$. In the next prime
band, $61\leq n\leq84$, the bound $\mathcal N(11)=4040/9$
exceeds every available value of $2n$.
Nevertheless, Theorem~\ref{thm:parameter-density-positive} can still
apply outside those ranges. At $n=30$, $P=\Pi(n)=35$, its two sides
are $40/7$ and $5$. At $n=77$, $P=\Pi(n)=385$, they are $900/77$
and $11$. Thus the residue-sensitive criterion proves positivity
in both cases.

Asymptotically, put $x=2n$ and let $p$ be the greatest prime not
exceeding $\sqrt{x}$. The prime number theorem implies
$p\sim\sqrt{x}$, and hence
\[
\log\mathcal N(p)\sim
2(\log3)\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\log x},
\qquad
\frac{\log\mathcal N(p)}{\log x}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Thus $x\geq\mathcal N(p)$ fails for all sufficiently large $x$
at this cutoff. The polynomial sieve scales in
Remark~\ref{rem:sieve-comparison} also do not reach $x\asymp p^2$.
The results of this paper do not establish
$g_{\Pi(n)}(2n)>0$ for every $n\geq13$.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
